To really protect animals, the most important thing is to look after the forests, rivers and seas where they live. And you can learn a lot about them from documentaries, books and visits to sanctuaries. People who say animals live well in zoos care about how the animals live; so, to be fair, they should also care about how animals living free in nature live.

text.bold: 6. A consistency test: if the criterion is welfare, it applies to everyone.

paragraph.text: A common version of the argument says animals "live longer" or "live better" in zoos, away from predators, hunger and disease. In part, this has a basis: a 2016 study of more than 50 mammal species found that most live longer in zoos than in the wild. But there are important exceptions: zoo elephants, for example, lived much shorter lives than wild ones according to a 2008 study. And living longer isn't the same as living well. The point here, though, isn't to settle who is right about the numbers, but to notice what this argument presupposes. Whoever uses it adopts the welfare of each individual as the criterion, not the mere existence of the species. If that is the criterion, two things follow:

text.bold: It applies to every zoo animal.

paragraph.text: The zoo is then judged by the life of each animal, including those who suffer from confinement, and not by the number of species preserved.

text.bold: It also applies to wild animals.

paragraph.text: If hunger, disease and predation in nature count against life in the wild, then the suffering of the billions of animals living in nature should matter too, and not only when it serves to defend captivity. This is the problem of

This isn't about accusing anyone of bad faith, but about proposing a test: those who take the welfare of zoo animals seriously are invited to take seriously the welfare of those living outside zoos too. If someone only invokes suffering in nature to justify confinement, the real criterion may not be welfare.

text.bold: 7. The same principles apply beyond food.

paragraph.text: , Peter Singer focuses his analysis on food and experiments, but includes zoos, alongside circuses, bullfights, hunting and the fur and pet trades, among the practices where the principle of equal consideration of interests has consequences. For him, the philosophical problems aren't very different, and it is up to the reader to apply the same principles (ch. 3). Applied to the zoo, this means asking whether each animal's interest in moving, exploring and living with others of their kind is weighed as seriously as the visitors' interest in seeing them and the goals of conservation (point 1).

text.bold: 8. Four questions for any use justified by an end.

paragraph.text: The philosopher Nathan Nobis proposes a checklist that applies to zoos, rodeos, hunting and other uses defended by what they produce: (1) is the end legitimate? (2) is using animals an effective means, or the most effective one, to reach it? (3) are there better means, without harm? (4) what are the best reasons to think that this end justifies a harm we would never accept imposing on humans? (

, 2016, pp. 70–71). Applied to the zoo, conservation and education are legitimate ends, and the first question is passed. The second is empirical and contested. A study funded by the American association of zoos and aquariums (Falk et al., 2007) reported that a visit strengthens attitudes favourable to conservation. A critical evaluation (Marino et al., 2010), co-authored by Nobis himself, pointed to methodological flaws, such as asking visitors whether they had learned instead of measuring what they learned, and concluded that there was no compelling evidence of attitude change; the authors of the original study published a reply. A later survey of about 5,600 visitors to 26 zoos and aquariums in 19 countries found a modest increase in understanding of biodiversity, from 69.8% to 75.1% of respondents, without measuring behaviour change (Moss, Jensen and Gusset, 2015). The third question weighs more: documentaries, sanctuaries, observation in the wild and habitat protection (point 3) teach and conserve without keeping animals confined for display. And the fourth remains unanswered as long as the argument only shows that the end is good.
